column13: For the First Respondent, the Tribunal found it just and equitable to extend time. The allegations were serious, the delay caused minimal prejudice to the Respondent and had limited effect on the cogency of evidence. The Claimant acted reasonably promptly to begin Early Conciliation once she received notification of the Stage 3 appeal outcome. She was trying to avoid litigation by exhausting the internal process. When taken with her vulnerability due to disability and the lack of or incorrect advice she received, it was just and equitable to extend time under section 123(1). For the Second Respondent, the Tribunal refused to extend time because Early Conciliation was entered into over one month later and the explanation (awaiting ACAS call back) was not convincing. The Second Respondent is not a legal entity and claims against it were unlikely to succeed as a matter of law. It was not just and equitable to extend time for claims with no prospect of success. For the Third Respondent, the Tribunal refused to extend time because the Third Respondent did not employ the Claimant, was only involved in the Stage 3 appeal, there was no claim of discrimination in relation to the Stage 3 appeal, and all allegations related to the First Respondent's conduct. Any claim against the Third Respondent would be likely to fail, so it was not just and equitable to extend time.

column13: The tribunal acknowledged that the Claimant's lack of knowledge of the emails until 8/11 April 2024 was a highly relevant factor. However, the tribunal found no basis to extend time. The Claimant had notified ACAS on 27 March 2024 (before receiving the emails), was represented by her Trade Union by early May 2024, and was supported by her husband. She participated in her appeal hearing on 8 May 2024. The tribunal found that the Claimant could reasonably have submitted her claim shortly after 11 April 2024 rather than waiting until 17 July 2024. Her explanation that it was a difficult time did not amount to a good reason, particularly given the support available to her. The tribunal noted there is a public interest in applying time limits strictly and that extension is the exception rather than the rule. While the tribunal found no significant prejudice to the Respondent (as the claim rested on three uncontested emails), this alone was not a reason to extend time.

column13: The tribunal accepted the claimant's evidence that she was aware of the deadline and believed she had met it. The tribunal accepted her evidence that the reason she was wrong was to do with the way in which she is impacted by ADHD. The delay was less than three weeks. There was no prejudice to the respondent in answering the claim other than the fact of having to answer a claim that is outside of the usual time limits. There was no evidence before the tribunal that would have enabled it to consider merit. The tribunal concluded that where it accepted the claimant's evidence that her ability to comply with the deadlines was affected by her ADHD, where if it decided not to extend time the claimant would lose the opportunity to bring her claim of race discrimination, and where there was no forensic prejudice to the respondent, it would be just and equitable to extend time for the filing of this claim to 11 June 2024.

column13: The tribunal considered whether it was just and equitable to extend time. The claims were six months late. The claimant had knowledge of all relevant facts by 15 May 2023. The tribunal found no reasonable explanation for the delay, given the claimant's intelligence, union membership, and unique knowledge from working in an Employment Tribunal. The tribunal considered prejudice to both parties: the claimant would lose her claims, but the respondent faced prejudice from the passage of time affecting cogency of evidence (witnesses unable to recall events eight months later), and some witnesses had left employment and were reluctant. On merits, the tribunal found the claims weak: the claimant failed safety-critical tests three times in accordance with prescribed procedures; comparators were in materially different circumstances (Witness X raised menopause symptoms; others involved different misconduct); statistics showed 32 of 37 who failed tests were dismissed, including a broad mix by sex, race and age. The tribunal concluded the claims were not strong enough to make it just and equitable to extend time.

column13: The tribunal declined to extend time on a just and equitable basis. The claimant knew at all times that she could bring the claim. The triggering event in February 2024 demonstrated that the claimant chose to delay bringing her claim and proceeded at least in part because of her perception about the way others were treated. There was considerable delay. The passage of time could cause difficulties for the respondent in obtaining evidence, with relevant witnesses having limited memory or having moved on. The respondent did not contribute to any delay. The tribunal found that the claimant chose not to bring her claim but has now changed her mind. The tribunal rejected the argument that she had been inhibited by mental health, as it was not supported by adequate medical evidence and was inconsistent with her ability to work. The tribunal did not find it just and equitable to extend time.

column13: The Tribunal found it just and equitable to extend time. The delay was only 7 weeks (49 days). The cogency of evidence would not be affected by such a short delay, as the case turns on documentary evidence (Access to Work Report and grievance outcome letter) rather than witness recollection. The claimant acted on professional advice throughout, including incorrect advice from her union. She pursued an internal grievance before issuing proceedings, which was a reasonable step. The respondent itself caused persistent delays in making adjustments and handling the grievance. The claim has good prospects of success as the respondent admitted in the grievance outcome that it failed to make reasonable adjustments. The balance of prejudice favoured the claimant: refusing an extension would prevent her pursuing a meritorious claim, while granting it would not prevent the respondent defending but merely remove a windfall defence. The Tribunal cited Hawkins v Ball and British Coal Corporation v Keeble, noting that incorrect advice from advisors can support a just and equitable extension in discrimination claims.

column13: The tribunal found that the claimant's ignorance of time limits was reasonable in the circumstances. She had taken steps to resolve the matter through the respondent's internal grievance procedure after reading information on the gov.uk website and speaking to ACAS, which left her with the impression that she should follow the internal process first. She had an understandable expectation that the grievance would be addressed promptly (within 20 days as per policy). The respondent's extremely lengthy delay (16 months) in addressing her grievance was not caused by the claimant and was unreasonable for an organisation of the respondent's size and resources. Once the claimant was informed of time limits by ACAS on 18 July 2023, she acted promptly, commencing early conciliation within two days. The tribunal found that the claimant's ignorance of time limits was reasonable and that once informed, she acted without further delay. The tribunal concluded that the unreasonable delay in dealing with the claimant's grievance effectively caused the claimant to present her claim out of time. The prejudice to the claimant (losing the ability to bring her claim entirely) outweighed the prejudice to the respondent (general prejudice of facing a time-barred claim). There was no evidence of specific forensic prejudice, and the respondent had investigated the complaints during the grievance process and had ready access to relevant documentation. The tribunal was unable to conclude that the claim had no real merit on the limited information available. The tribunal found that it was just and equitable to extend time to allow the claim to proceed.

The claimant's reason (trying to persuade the respondent to address complaints internally) was not considered a good reason for extending time. The length of delay was not substantial and unlikely to impact the cogency of evidence, but the claimant had not given a good reason for the delay. The poor prospects of success of the claim was a further reason for refusing to extend time. The Tribunal concluded it was not just and equitable to extend time.

The tribunal noted that whilst there might be hurdles to overcome (different wrongdoers, lengthy period of time), it could not be said on the material provided that there was no reasonable prospect of success. The tribunal stated that the evidential basis for the claims had not been considered, and that the tribunal would need to hear the evidence and decide the jurisdiction point as part of the final hearing. The tribunal emphasised its wide discretion in extending the relevant time limit and noted that the reason for the timing of the presentation of the claim is important, and that physical and/or mental health might have played a part. The tribunal noted that crucial facts were disputed and there had been no opportunity for the evidence to be considered, including evidence on timing. The tribunal refused to speculate on the nature or strength of evidence to be provided at the final hearing.

The tribunal acknowledged the claimant's mental health problems but found no medical evidence was provided. The tribunal believed the claimant had mental health problems of varying severity but was not persuaded these were in themselves a reasonable or sufficient explanation for not taking steps to pursue a claim. The extension sought was significant (approximately 9 months after expiry, 12 months after resignation, 22 months after the Christmas party). The respondent was prejudiced by Mr X leaving in April 2024 and Mr Y leaving in September 2023, with evidence not secured. The tribunal found the factors of significant length of extension, lack of positive steps by the claimant, and prejudice to the respondent outweighed the claimant's explanation based on ill health and her wish to bring serious allegations. The tribunal concluded it was not just and equitable to extend time.

The tribunal referred to Robertson v Bexley Community Centre, noting that the exercise of discretion to extend time is the exception rather than the rule and the burden of proof is on the claimant to show why time should be extended. The tribunal found: 'I understand that the claimant is a litigant in person, but he had not made any attempt to explain the delay even in lay terms. Also, the claimant does appear to have had some legal advice. The claimant had not presented evidence to the Tribunal as to why time should be extended on the just and equitable basis. Accordingly, the Tribunal does not exercise its discretion to extend time, and the claim is out of time.'

column13: The tribunal dismissed the discrimination claims on multiple grounds. Most claims were found to be res judicata: either cause of action estoppel (where the same cause of action had been determined in 2022 proceedings), issue estoppel (where findings made in 2022 were binding on the same issue), or Henderson abuse of process (where claims could and should have been raised in the 2022 proceedings). For claims not caught by res judicata, the tribunal found them substantially out of time (dating from 2018-2023, with claim forms presented in August 2024). The tribunal repeatedly stated: 'The claimant has not provided any grounds on which it is just and equitable to extend time limits. On the basis the burden of proof is on the claimant, and I have not been presented with any reasons why the complaint is being presented now, or any argument about a continuing act, I dismiss the complaint as presented out of time, the time limits cannot be extended.' The claimant did not attend to give evidence or make submissions on extension of time. One in-time claim (4.2.5 - removal of training number) was struck out as having no reasonable prospect of success given the 2022 judgment findings.

column13: The Tribunal refused the Respondent's application to strike out the pre-4 August 2023 discrimination claims on time grounds. The Tribunal held that the Claimant had respectable arguments that: (1) the succession of bonus decisions were manifestations of a practice or policy motivated by discrimination and properly seen as conduct extending over a period under s123(3)(a) Equality Act 2010; (2) unlawful bonus decisions take effect when the deferred element is paid (April following declaration), meaning time ran from April 2023 for the April 2023 bonus, bringing claims comfortably within time; (3) if the bonus-based conduct extending over a period argument succeeded, the denial of Vice President status and forcible transfer claims could also be in time as further instances of the continuing discriminatory state of affairs. The Tribunal found the Claimant's case was nowhere near hopeless and had respectable arguments, falling very far short of having no reasonable prospect of success. On the just and equitable extension under s123(1)(b), the Tribunal held that even if the conduct extending over a period argument failed, the Claimant had reasonable prospects of persuading the Tribunal to exercise its broad discretion to extend time. Relevant factors would include: length of delay (which could not be determined at this stage and might be minor if time ran from April 2023); the Claimant's mental health (her case would need to be tested in cross-examination with medical evidence, but there was no reason to assume it would not be accepted); and prejudice to the Respondent (which could not be assessed without knowing the extent of delay). The Tribunal concluded the Respondent's arguments on just and equitable extension were even more difficult than on conduct extending over a period because there was no firm premise from which to start. The Tribunal emphasised it had made no factual findings and reached its conclusions without regard to oral evidence, applying the correct legal test for strike-out under rule 38(1)(a) of the Employment Tribunals Rules of Procedure 2024.

column13: The Tribunal refused the application to extend time on just and equitable grounds. (4) The delay had impacted the claimant's memory and the cogency of evidence is likely to be affected, as evidenced by contradictions between the claimant's oral evidence and contemporaneous documentary evidence. (5) The claimant had sought advice from multiple sources since 2021 and his continued ignorance of the law was not reasonable, particularly after the Tribunal had informed him it did not have jurisdiction over his first claim.

column13: Claims relating to acts or omissions before 7 June 2023 are out of time. The Tribunal refused to extend time on just and equitable grounds for most discrimination claims. The claimant was an experienced Employee Relations Officer fully aware of the 3-month time limit and that discrimination claims could be brought during employment. Her explanation that she was 'scared' to bring claims while employed was not found plausible given she had made a protected disclosure in December 2021 and appeared as a witness in a colleague's discrimination case in November 2018. The Tribunal applied the principle from Concentrix v Obi that it is not required to take an 'all or nothing approach' and may extend time only for the most recent incidents to avoid forensic prejudice. The Tribunal allowed only specific allegations from January 2022 to August 2023 involving Mr Ceesay's alleged disdainful treatment and Ms Jackson's conduct at the appeal hearing on 17 August 2023 to proceed as continuing acts or on just and equitable grounds.

column13: The tribunal applied the just and equitable test under section 123 Equality Act 2010. The tribunal found the claimant had not satisfied the burden of demonstrating that time should be extended. The claimant relied almost exclusively on purported verbal advice from an ACAS officer that she had a further week beyond a calendar month to submit her claim, but failed to check the accuracy of that remark with two advisory services she approached and failed to undertake her own research online. The tribunal found the claimant had access to advice from CAB and her trade union, and ample advice was available online. The tribunal also considered the balance of prejudice. The claimant had not provided sufficient factual information to clarify her discrimination claim, putting the respondent at a disadvantage. The delay in submitting and clarifying the claim impacted the cogency of evidence and the respondent's ability to recall and preserve evidence. The tribunal also noted that, taking the claimant's case at its best, the respondent had a very good prospect of objectively justifying any decision not to proceed with her employment if her medical condition caused her not to attend flight schedules on time, given the industrial context and the importance of punctuality. The tribunal concluded it was not just and equitable to extend time.

column13: All direct race discrimination claims were manifestly out of time, most well over 2 years and the earliest 5 months out of time. The Tribunal found the Claimant had not discharged the burden of persuading the Tribunal to exercise its discretion to extend time. The Tribunal also found, on the merits, no evidence that any alleged acts were in any way tainted by race or national origin.

column13: The tribunal refused to extend time under the just and equitable test. column13: The tribunal refused to extend time under the just and equitable test. Key factors: (1) Length of delay was significant (over 3 months, longer than the primary time limit itself). (2) Reasons for delay were not compelling: although the claimant was unwell, she was able to prepare a detailed 22-page grievance in February 2023 which she later used as her claim form, undermining her assertion she was too unwell to claim earlier; she knew or should have known about time limits from early January 2023. (3) Prejudice to respondent was very significant: 15-day hearing listed, many witnesses required, 800-page bundle for preliminary hearing alone, publicly funded respondent facing substantial costs, claimant unrepresented with significant health issues making preparation difficult. (4) Forensic prejudice was substantial: complaints dated back to October 2014 (over 10 years), with numerous complaints throughout 2021-2022; witnesses would be cross-examined about events many years earlier at a January 2026 hearing. (5) Prejudice to claimant was acknowledged but merits appeared doubtful: complaints were confused and in some respects hopeless; respondent made repeated redeployment efforts; claimant was pursuing separate personal injury litigation for loss of entire nursing career which could yield significant compensation. The tribunal considered but rejected limiting the claim to November-December 2022 complaints only, finding this would provide relatively modest benefit and would likely require contextual evidence covering the entire chronology anyway.

column13: The tribunal concluded it was not just and equitable to extend time for the discrimination claims. The tribunal found the delays (ranging from approximately 5 to 8 months) to be very significant. The tribunal did not find the claimant's explanation that she was unfamiliar with tribunal procedure to be credible, particularly given that she had worked in HR for many years and had made reference to pursuing an Employment Tribunal claim in a GP consultation on 3 May 2022. The tribunal noted that the claimant had been in contact with ACAS (as evidenced by a handwritten note dated 27 June 2024) and had commenced early conciliation on 28 August 2024, indicating she was capable of taking steps to pursue a claim. The tribunal was not provided with medical evidence to support a finding that the claimant was too unwell to pursue a claim during the relevant period. The tribunal found that, although it may not have been without difficulty, it would have been possible for the claimant to have issued proceedings at a much earlier date. The tribunal balanced the prejudice to the respondent of having to answer historic allegations where memories fade and extensive documentation must be retrieved, and noted the lack of particularity regarding the timing of various events. The tribunal emphasised that extending time is the exception rather than the rule.

column13: The tribunal considered whether to grant an extension of time for two additional allegations (harassment related to disability on 4 September 2024 and victimisation on 31 July 2024) which were 11 and 13 months out of time respectively. The tribunal refused the amendment application for these allegations, noting: (1) the allegations were not in the original detailed narrative filed with the ET1; (2) the claimant had already had an opportunity to amend her claim at the previous preliminary hearing when EJ Young extracted clarification and set out the List of Issues; (3) there would be some prejudice from loss of cogency of evidence with passage of time; (4) there would be cost to the respondent in amending the response and gathering evidence; (5) the essence of the claimant's case was already set out in the List of Issues; (6) the claimant did not really need further expansion of her case. The tribunal also refused to make a deposit order, finding it could not assess merit without hearing evidence, noting the claimant's case of a prevailing culture of disregarding her disabilities, and finding she had reasonable prospect of persuading the tribunal it was just and equitable to extend time for the harassment allegation about the 'fuck wit' remark.

column13: The tribunal found that the discrimination claims dated 22 and 25 February 2022 were prima facie out of time (before 1 October 2022). The tribunal noted its wide discretion, the lack of evidential prejudice to the respondent (who was able to call witnesses and defend its position), the claimant's neurodivergence, his lack of advice on time limits, his affected mental health, and the fact that without an extension the claimant would have no redress for discriminatory treatment. The tribunal stated: 'The Tribunal determined it was just and equitable to extend time... on the basis of just and equitable principles. The discretion of the Tribunal in extending time is wide. The claimant who is neurodivergent did not obtain advice on time limits and his mental health was affected by his treatment necessitating an increase in medication. Of significance is the lack of prejudice by the respondent in extending time; it has been able to call evidence of a direct witness to events (and had the availability to call other witnesses if it chose to do so) and defend its position. If time is not extended for this claimant he will have no redress for his discriminatory treatment.'

column13: The tribunal refused to extend time for out-of-time discrimination claims on just and equitable grounds. Reasons: (1) substantial delays (minimum 5 months, maximum over 18 months); (2) claimant was aware she could bring tribunal proceedings (expressly raised possibility in November 2019); (3) claimant chose not to bring proceedings after receiving positive response to adjustment requests in November 2019, only deciding to pursue claims months later when unrelated disputes arose; (4) parties had resolved all adjustment requests by November 2019 and it would not be just and equitable to reopen resolved disputes; (5) clear evidential gaps, particularly for older complaints, with relevant employees having left. The tribunal also found the complaints did not amount to a continuing act: they arose on separate occasions involving many different individuals, with no senior employee 'pulling the strings', and a clear line was drawn in November 2019. The in-time harassment and victimisation claims were dismissed on merits: the instruction to log on early and the disciplinary action were not related to disability.

column13: The tribunal found it just and equitable to extend time for the harassment and failure to make reasonable adjustments claims. The claimant was trying to resolve matters internally and had raised his complaints with his employer as part of that process. His claim form was issued on 4 December 2023, within three months of the termination of his employment and after he had received the outcome of the grievance. The tribunal took into account the nature of the claimant's disabilities (ADHD and dyslexia), which make it more difficult for him to focus and deal with paperwork. The claimant had not put his mind to time limits whilst going through the internal grievance procedures. Although he had a union representative, the focus was on achieving a resolution internally. The claimant thought he was doing the right thing by focussing first on the internal procedures and in all the circumstances that was reasonable. The prejudice to the respondent was not significant as it was able to investigate the allegations as part of the grievance process and these were documented in records available to the respondent. The prejudice to the claimant would be that he could not make any complaint under the Equality Act and this outweighed any prejudice to the respondent.

column13: The Tribunal accepted the Claimant's evidence that he did not know about the discriminatory policy until June 2023 and had no reason to suspect discrimination earlier. The Tribunal found the Claimant to be an honest and compelling witness. The news stories in August 2022 and February 2023 were less impactful than those in June 2023, which followed the internal investigation and public statement confirming the discriminatory policy. The Claimant acted promptly once aware, filing a service complaint on 11 July 2023 and initiating Early Conciliation on 27 July 2023. Although the delay was considerable (especially for the 2020 application), much of the evidence had been preserved in the Respondent's internal investigation and the Claimant's applications appeared to be a matter of documentary record, limiting prejudice to the Respondent. The Tribunal also noted that the documents suggested there were questions to be answered by the Respondent. column13: The tribunal exercised its discretion to extend time on the basis that it was just and equitable. The delay was approximately 3 months and 2 weeks (ignoring early conciliation), which was not considered significant in the context of this case. The claimant's mental health deteriorated around the anniversaries of his son's birthday (11 November) and Christmas, which accounted for a significant portion of the delay. He raised a grievance on 25 January 2024 and commenced early conciliation on 8 February 2024, only 2 weeks after the grievance and 2 days after its outcome. The period during early conciliation (until 21 March 2024) could not be held against him. The claim was presented 12 days after the first early conciliation ended, which was considered reasonable given his mental health. The respondent's assertion of prejudice was unpersuasive; there was no specific evidence of memory difficulties beyond the usual passage of time, and the claim involved mostly one manager. Although the claimant could have reasonably discovered the time limit (including through his wife, who had HR knowledge), this did not outweigh the other circumstances, particularly his mental health and the impact of the anniversaries.

column12: length_of_delay; prejudice; illness; mental_health; lack_of_advice; internal_grievance; ignorance_of_rights; merits
column13: The Tribunal found no reasonable prospect that the out-of-time allegations (11 to 18, 35 to 41, 26 to 28) formed conduct extending over a period with the in-time allegations, given the gap of more than two years from August 2021 to November 2023, the discrete nature of the allegations, and the involvement of different people. For whistleblowing detriment allegations (11 to 18), the Tribunal found no reasonable prospect that it was not reasonably practicable to present the claims in time. For all discrimination allegations, the Tribunal found no reasonable prospect that a just and equitable extension would be granted. The Tribunal weighed the forensic prejudice to the respondent (witnesses being asked to recall events 8, 7, 4, and 3 years previously, rising to 10, 9, 6, and 5 years by the time of hearing) against the prejudice to the claimant. The Tribunal noted that the claimant was a graduate, had returned to work after her 2016/2017 absence with employer-provided counselling, was working in 2020 and 2021, was a union member from 2018, overcame her fear to present a grievance in 2022, and knew of Tribunals by early 2023 through her husband's case. The Tribunal found that the claimant's reasons for delay (fear, health, focus on family, ignorance of rights) were insufficient to tip the balance of prejudice in her favour, particularly given that she had chosen to prioritise her husband's Tribunal case and had always had the opportunity to bring her allegations to the Tribunal. The Tribunal also noted that the claimant's path to remedy was uncertain given the complexity of establishing causation, and that her sense of justice for historic wrongs was mitigated by the employer's handling of her grievance being examined in the proceedings and by the substantial in-time case remaining.

column13: The Tribunal applied the just and equitable test. Although there were cogent reasons for the claimant's delay, particularly in the first four or five months following termination, the Tribunal found that the 18-month delay had so damaged the cogency of the evidence that a fair trial was no longer possible. There was almost no documentary evidence; the respondent's Teams messages were routinely deleted after 90 days; the claimant could not identify when he verbally informed the respondent of his health struggles or requested adjustments; and the respondent's witnesses had no recollection. The claimant's case relied on proving the respondent knew or ought to have known he was disabled during employment, but the lack of contemporaneous documents and the passage of time meant neither party could give their best evidence. The Tribunal concluded it would not be just and equitable to grant such a long extension of time.

column13: The tribunal found it was reasonably practicable for the claim to have been submitted in time. Although the claimant was recovering from a road traffic accident and taking painkillers, there was nearly a fortnight after the accident in which he had internet access and no evidence that his medical condition was sufficiently serious to prevent him from submitting the claim online. The tribunal applied a liberal interpretation in favour of the claimant but concluded it was reasonably practicable to have submitted the claim in time.

column13: The tribunal found it was reasonably practicable to have presented the claim within the initial three-month time limit. Although the claimant suffered poor mental health after dismissal and had no IT skills, the tribunal found his mental health was not such as to prevent him investigating how to make a claim. The reason he did not research time limits was that he expected his appeal to be successful. Once the appeal was rejected, he was able to consult the CAB, speak to ACAS, and find out how to make a claim with his father's help. The tribunal found he was able to take those steps before the appeal during the primary time limit and did not do so because he expected to be reinstated. The tribunal held that discovering the proper time limit is not difficult and a simple Google search or short call to ACAS or CAB would quickly reveal it. The tribunal also found that even if it had been not reasonably practicable, the claim was not presented within a reasonable time after expiry, as the claimant delayed three weeks after being advised by CAB and ACAS.

column13: The tribunal applied the just and equitable test. Each of the four heads of the discrimination claim included allegations current at the point of resignation. The tribunal was asked to extend time for a period of two months. The tribunal accepted that although ultimately incorrect, the claimant had good reason for believing the first respondent to be his employer. The claimant was unwell and unable to work from before his resignation until after the claim was filed. The respondents did not argue any specific or forensic prejudice. The tribunal found the claimant would suffer significant prejudice if not given permission to pursue the claim of disability discrimination, a prejudice greater than any to the second respondent, particularly where the second respondent would need to address many of the same issues in its response to the dismissal case. Time for filing the claim of disability discrimination was extended to 2 June 2024. The tribunal made no decision about whether allegations regarding incidents that took place more than three months prior to 27 March 2024 (the date ACAS was contacted) are in time or whether there was a continuing course of conduct; this is a matter for the final hearing.

column13: The tribunal applied the just and equitable test. Each of the four heads of the discrimination claim included allegations current at the point of resignation. The tribunal was asked to extend time for a period of two months. The tribunal accepted that although ultimately incorrect, the claimant had good reason for believing the first respondent to be his employer. The claimant was unwell and unable to work from before his resignation until after the claim was filed. The respondents did not argue any specific or forensic prejudice. The tribunal found the claimant would suffer significant prejudice if not given permission to pursue the claim of disability discrimination, a prejudice greater than any to the second respondent, particularly where the second respondent would need to address many of the same issues in its response to the dismissal case. Time for filing the claim of disability discrimination was extended to 2 June 2024. The tribunal made no decision about whether allegations regarding incidents that took place more than three months prior to 27 March 2024 (the date ACAS was contacted) are in time or whether there was a continuing course of conduct; this is a matter for the final hearing.

column13: The tribunal found it was reasonably practicable for the claimant to present her claim on time. The claimant was aware of the 3-month time limit at the time of ACAS early conciliation. Although she suffered from depression and was receiving talking therapy from August 2024 to August 2025, she was able to function sufficiently to undertake reasonably involved tasks during the limitation period, including writing her resignation letter, seeking advice from CAB, engaging with ACAS, taking training courses, and presenting her claim. The impact of her depression was not so detrimental as to render it not reasonably practicable to present her claim in time. With respect to waiting for a resolution, ACAS early conciliation ended in February 2025, putting her on notice that resolution was unlikely, and there was no evidence of negotiations thereafter. This was not sufficient reason to delay presenting her claim.

column13: The tribunal applied the just and equitable test under section 123(1)(b) Equality Act 2010. The tribunal found the claimant had no compelling reason for late presentation. The tribunal noted that at a previous case management hearing on 24 September 2025, the claimant was told he needed to identify a protected act to pursue a victimisation claim and that a protected act involves an allegation of breach of the Equality Act 2010. The claimant had not identified any protected act within the meaning of section 27 of the Equality Act 2010 and declined to withdraw the claim. The tribunal found the victimisation claim could not succeed in the absence of an identified protected act. The tribunal found the prejudice to the respondent in having to answer a hopeless claim was greater than the prejudice to the claimant in not being able to pursue such a claim. The tribunal therefore found it was not just and equitable to extend time.

(9) Even after receiving the Acas certificate on 5 August 2024, the claimant waited a further 18 days before issuing her claim. The tribunal concluded there was no jurisdiction to hear the claim and it must be struck out.

column13: The Tribunal applied the two-stage test under s111(2)(b) ERA: (1) whether it was not reasonably practicable for the claim to be presented in time, and (2) if not, whether it was presented within a reasonable further period. The Tribunal found it was reasonably practicable for the claimant to have presented his claim by 30 January 2024. The Tribunal rejected the claimant's belief that he had to complete the internal grievance process as unreasonable, finding no policy or communication from the respondent supported this. The Tribunal found the claimant was well enough to work throughout the limitation period and was capable of undertaking the research needed to find out the time limits, as evidenced by his detailed legal research in his complaint letter of 16 June 2024. The Tribunal also found the claim was not presented within a reasonable further period, as the claimant waited until 4 November 2024 without any change in circumstances that would have lifted the alleged impediments.

column13: The tribunal applied the just and equitable test under s. 123 of the Equality Act. The tribunal found the length of the delay was significant (approximately 8.5 months). The reasons for delay were poorly explained, certainly beyond April 2024. There was no suggestion that the claimant did not have all the relevant facts to enable her to bring a claim earlier. She had sought advice from solicitors and an accountant and had been left in no doubt that what the respondent had done was wrong. There was no suggestion that she had not realised that she had a right of action. She simply seemed to have dragged her feet. Many of the acts of discrimination occurred long before 5 July 2023 and the claimant simply did not demonstrate a good reason for the discretion within s. 123 to have been exercised in her favour. The tribunal also took into account the claimant's conduct during the hearing, which was abusive and intemperate despite repeated warnings.

column13: The Tribunal found it was reasonably practicable for the Claimant to have presented his claims in time. The Claimant was in a position to and did seek advice from several sources within the first three months about an unfair dismissal claim. He either misunderstood the advice he received (to wait for his appeal outcome, after which he would still have had around a month to contact ACAS) or he was wrongly advised that he could not bring the claim until the criminal investigation was concluded. The lawyers should reasonably have given him advice that the time limit starts to run on the effective date of termination and that he should not delay because of the ongoing criminal investigation. The Claimant's ignorance or mistaken belief of when the time limits started to run was not reasonable, even if he was wrongly advised. His active steps to get advice and find out the position showed he was capable of also presenting his claim. The Tribunal applied Wall's Meat Co Ltd v Khan [1979] ICR 53, holding that ignorance or mistaken belief will not be reasonable if it arises from the fault of a claimant's solicitors or other professional advisers in not giving such information as they should reasonably have given. English not being his first language did not prevent him from researching and contacting multiple sources of advice.

The tribunal rejected the claimant's arguments that his mental health, the ongoing appeal, or other factors made it not reasonably feasible to present the claim in time. The medical evidence did not establish that the claimant was unable to present a claim or research time limits during the relevant period. The claimant was able to engage in correspondence, attend appeal hearings, and work as a security analyst from 2 February 2025. The tribunal concluded it was reasonably practicable (reasonably feasible) for the claimant to have presented his claims by 13 March 2025, and therefore had no power to extend time.

column13: The tribunal found it was reasonably practicable for the claimant to have presented the claim in time. The claimant was an intelligent, articulate, successful businessman with access to the internet, professional legal advice from a solicitor (Mr Smith), and informal HR advice from a friend. He was aware of his right to bring an Employment Tribunal claim and was actively contesting his dismissal through the internal appeal process. The tribunal held it was reasonable to expect him to have made enquiries about the correct time limit, either through his own research or by asking his professional advisers. His reliance on unspecified 'word of mouth' information was unreasonable given his professional background and the importance of the matter. Although the tribunal acknowledged the impact of his wife's medical situation (investigations and diagnosis of breast cancer from late June to 19 July 2024), it found this did not prevent him from filing the claim in time, particularly as the diagnosis occurred after the time limit had already expired. The tribunal concluded that the claimant's mistaken belief about the time limit was not reasonable in the circumstances.

column13: The tribunal found that it was reasonably practicable for the claimant to have presented his claim in time. The tribunal concluded it was not only possible but reasonable to expect the claimant to have submitted the claim within time.

column13: The tribunal applied the 'reasonably practicable' test under section 111(2) ERA 1996. The burden was on the claimant to show it was not reasonably practicable to present the claim in time. The tribunal found that the claimant had a smartphone and it was almost inconceivable that he would not make enquiries about his rights if he believed he had suffered an injustice. His failure to make enquiries until summer 2024 did not mean it was not reasonably practicable to present the claim earlier. The tribunal also found it unlikely that the trade union and MP gave no information about tribunal claims. The tribunal noted that typing 'unfair dismissal' into a search engine brings up the Gov.uk website on rights. The claimant was able to contact ACAS when he put his mind to it, but his failure to do so before September 2024 was fatal. The delay between obtaining the conciliation certificate on 7 October 2024 and presenting the ET1 on 1 November 2024 was also found not to be reasonable. The tribunal concluded that the claim was presented out of time when it was reasonably practicable to have presented it in time, and the claimant could not benefit from the ACAS EC extension.

column13: The Tribunal found that the Claimant had not proved it was not reasonably practicable to present his complaint in time. The Tribunal considered not only what the Claimant knew but what he ought to have known, taking into account sources of information available to him. The Tribunal gave particular weight to: the Claimant being highly educated with undergraduate and postgraduate qualifications in law; assistance from Mr Grieve (a former Detective Superintendent) from at least two months before dismissal; contact with Citizens' Advice by 12 March 2024; reference to Employment Tribunals and 'unfair dismissal' in correspondence before the deadline; and support from a retired HR professional. The Tribunal accepted the Claimant had PTSD but found it did not prevent completion of an ET1 form, given the robust manner in which he conducted his appeal. The Tribunal rejected the Claimant's submission that the Respondent should have told him about his right to take legal proceedings, and did not accept his evidence that he delayed for fear of harming the Respondent's reputation. Even accepting the appeal process delayed matters, the outcome was communicated on 27 March 2024, still allowing time to submit the claim within the required time limit. The Tribunal also found that a further delay of 57 days was not a 'reasonable period' under the second limb of the test.

column13: The tribunal applied the 'just and equitable' test under section 123(1)(b) EQA 2010. The tribunal balanced prejudice to both parties. Prejudice to the claimant was considerable as she would be deprived of a claim. Prejudice to the respondent was equally considerable: events were almost 2 years old; oral testimony would be crucial; the principal witness (MRP) had left employment; trial was unlikely for at least another 9 months; the passage of time would significantly impact the cogency and credibility of oral evidence. The tribunal also considered: (1) the length of delay (approximately 10 months); (2) the claimant knew of the facts by 26 April 2023; (3) she did not accept she was unaware of tribunals; (4) she had opportunity to make enquiries but did not until October 2023; (5) no cogent evidence for delay from October 2023 to February 2024; (6) she was not deceived or misled; (7) health and bereavement did not significantly impact her ability to contact third parties or complete documentation; (8) no medical evidence of incapacity; (9) the IRM process was irrelevant as it was not akin to a grievance process. Balancing all factors, the tribunal concluded it should not exercise its discretion to extend time.

column13: The tribunal found it was not reasonably practicable for the claimant to present his claim within the time limit. The claimant, a litigant in person, relied heavily on Acas advice. Although he received the first Acas certificate on 12 February 2024 stating he had 'at least 1 month' to claim, this wording did not alert him to any strict time limit. He was confused about the relationship between Acas and the Employment Tribunal, believing them to be the same organisation. Before the one-month period expired, he received further communication from Acas on 29 February 2024 indicating conciliation was ongoing, reinforced by his Trade Union on 28 March 2024. The tribunal noted that the first certificate may have been issued in error as conciliation was still ongoing. The claimant only realised settlement would not be reached on 30 May 2024. Acas contacted him again on 14 June 2024 promising a certificate within 5 days, which was issued on 18 June 2024. He presented his claim the following day, 19 June 2024. The tribunal found the various conflicting communications from Acas caused significant confusion for the unfamiliar claimant, and it was not reasonable to expect him to present his claim within a month of the first certificate. The tribunal considered the further period (presenting the claim within one day of the second certificate) to be reasonable.

It accepted the respondent's submission that the last act of indirect discrimination was 13 March 2024, when the claimant went on long-term sickness absence and the working pattern policy ceased to apply to her. The claim was lodged approximately six months later. The tribunal found that despite her personal difficulties, the claimant was able to attend meetings, obtain new employment, communicate with her new employer, complete hardship fund applications, and participate in counselling. She had trade union support and could have sought guidance but did not. The tribunal balanced the prejudice to the claimant against the prejudice to the respondent in defending a claim concerning matters over 12 months old. It concluded there was no just and equitable basis to extend time.

Alternatively, even if the effective date had been 05 December 2023, the tribunal would have found it was not reasonably practicable to present the claim in time because the claimant reasonably believed she had been dismissed with one month's notice based on the dismissal letter and ACAS guidance, and she acted promptly on that reasonable belief by contacting ACAS on 03 April 2024 (the latest date consistent with a one-month notice period ending 04 January 2024). The tribunal rejected the argument that pursuing an internal appeal made it not reasonably practicable to claim in time.

column13: The tribunal found the unfair dismissal claim was dismissed primarily because the claimant did not have 2 years continuous service (employed 7 October 2022 to 10 December 2022 on claimant's dates, or 9 September 2022 to 28 September 2022 on respondent's dates). The tribunal also found the claim was out of time, presented nearly 16 months late. The claimant's explanation (identity theft and fraud causing administrative oversight) was not sufficient to satisfy the reasonably practicable test under s.111(2) ERA 1996. The tribunal noted the claimant had been able to bring a previous claim in February 2023 and settle it in April 2023, suggesting it would have been reasonably practicable to bring the present claim by the March 2023 deadline. The claim would also have been struck out as vexatious because it was covered by a COT 3 settlement dated 26 April 2023 which barred claims arising from employment with the respondent or its termination.

column13: The race discrimination claims were struck out on the ground that they have no reasonable prospects of success, not on limitation grounds. The tribunal found the claimant was unable to articulate any coherent case as to why the treatment of him was related to race. The claimant's case appeared to be that he had blown the whistle, was younger, better paid and popular, and that those were the reasons for the detriments. Insofar as he mentioned race, he simply said that others in the workplace were from different countries (UAE, Egypt, Sudan, and others) and that there were racial/nationality differences between him and other people in the workforce. There was nothing other than the fact of racial/nationality difference on which the claimant relied. The tribunal found no reasonable prospect of a tribunal finding that the detriments were because of race simply because the claimant's colleagues were of different races/nationalities to him, citing Madarassy v Nomura.

column13: The tribunal found the discrimination and harassment claims had no reasonable prospect of success on merits. The tribunal struck out all allegations within the July Schedule. Regarding time limits, the tribunal noted Type 1 allegations (throughout employment, latest 16 April 2024) could have been brought in time, while Type 2 allegations (specific dates, latest February 2024) were all outside the primary time limit. The tribunal did not reach a final determination on whether time should be extended under the just and equitable test, as the claims were struck out on merits.

column13: The tribunal found the race discrimination claim was also out of time but exercised its discretion to extend time on just and equitable grounds. The delay was 11 days from the ACAS deadline (or 4 days from when the Claimant learned of the deadline on 20 June). The Claimant's explanation lacked insight but was not materially dishonest. The tribunal accepted that the Claimant was at fault for missing the deadline but noted he was dealing with significant life stressors: unforeseen job loss, difficulty obtaining new employment without a good reference, and responsibility for a young child preparing for serious surgery. column12: length_of_delay; prejudice; lack_of_advice; ignorance_of_rights; promptness; merits
column13: The tribunal declined to extend time on a just and equitable basis. For the linen porter claim (over 10 months late), the tribunal found prejudice to the respondent in defending allegations 13-18 months after the events when the respondent did not know there was a complaint. The claimant had not raised the issue during employment, in his grievance, or grievance appeal, suggesting it was not important to him. For the 'Nea Dan' claim (6 months late), the tribunal found the claimant had access to a trade union representative and mentioned contacting a lawyer in April 2023, so could have obtained advice on age discrimination law and time limits. The claim was not mentioned in the grievance or appeal only one month after the conduct stopped, suggesting it was not a pressing concern. The tribunal noted the claimant was not afraid to complain about other matters, so his failure to raise this at the time suggested he did not find it objectionable then. The balance of prejudice favoured the respondent.

column13: The tribunal granted an extension of time on just and equitable grounds for the discrimination claims relating to dismissal and the 19 December 2023 appeal outcome, and permitted amendment to add the 3 September 2024 grievance appeal outcome. The tribunal balanced the significant impact of the Claimant's mental health (PTSD, severe depression and anxiety diagnosed in February 2024, with deterioration from December 2023), her misunderstanding of time limits, her engagement in internal processes, and the relatively short delay (9-10 weeks for dismissal-related claims) against the prejudice to the Respondent. The tribunal found that although some witnesses had left employment and may be reluctant to give evidence, there were extensive contemporaneous documents and internal investigation reports. The Claimant would be denied a remedy if claims did not proceed, and her mental health had been significantly affected. The tribunal concluded the balance of prejudice favoured the Claimant. For the 3 September 2024 outcome, despite the longer delay (approximately 9 months out of time), the tribunal found the Respondent would need to address this outcome in defending other claims in any event, and the Claimant's mental health and misunderstanding of tribunal processes explained the delay. The tribunal made no determination on whether there was a continuing act of discrimination, deferring this to final hearing.
